# Generative Models as Transport: History and Validation {.unnumbered}

*The rigorous twin of [Moving Distributions: The Transport Story](./03-transport-story.qmd).
This tutorial states the transport view of generative modeling precisely, traces
its history, and validates — or corrects — each of its claims against theorems
and the literature. Every load-bearing citation below was checked against its
source; the two adversarial review passes that shaped this document flagged, in
particular, two category errors that the folklore version of the thesis commits,
and both are repaired here.*

## The thesis, and two category errors to avoid

The folklore version of the transport view says: *generative modeling is
fundamentally transport; in 1-D the inverse CDF solves it completely and all
model families coincide there; in higher dimension the transport is no longer
unique, and VAEs, GANs, flows, and diffusion models are different general
constructions.* This is close to right — and wrong in two instructive ways.

**Category error 1: representation is not explanation.** On standard Borel
spaces, *essentially every* distribution is the pushforward of a uniform random
variable by some measurable map; a stochastic sampler becomes a deterministic
one after adjoining its auxiliary noise to the source. "Every generative model
is a transport" is therefore nearly tautological — a *representation* available
for anything, not a characterization of anything. What the transport language
genuinely does not capture: tractability of the **likelihood** (flows buy it
with Jacobians, the probability-flow ODE with divergence integration, VAEs with
an evidence bound, GANs not at all); **conditioning** (a coherent family
$p(dx \mid c)$ is more structure than an endpoint map); **stochastic kernels**
(a VAE decoder is a Markov kernel, not a map, and its encoder approximates a
posterior kernel, not an inverse); and — decisively for what follows —
**coupling identification**: two maps can have identical pushforwards and
completely different input–output correspondences. Matching the endpoint law
does not identify the map.

**Category error 2: 1-D uniqueness is a property of a *selection rule*, not of
dimension.** Even on the real line, transport is wildly nonunique: both
$u \mapsto u$ and $u \mapsto 1-u$ carry $\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$ to itself, and
composing any generator with a source-preserving map changes nothing about the
output law. What dimension one possesses is a *uniquely privileged selection*:
the total order, and with it the requirement "order-preserving," which singles
out one map. Higher dimensions do not lose transport; they lose the privileged
tie-breaker.

With both corrections made, the thesis survives in a sharper form, stated at
the end of this tutorial. The body earns it.

## Dimension one: the complete theory of order-compatible transport

Fix probability measures $\mu, \nu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with CDFs
$F_\mu, F_\nu$ and quantile functions
$Q_\mu(u) = \inf\{x : F_\mu(x) \ge u\}$ (generalized inverses, defined for
*all* laws, atoms included).

**Fact 1 (generation always works — atoms included).** $Q_{\nu\#}\,
\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1) = \nu$ for *every* law $\nu$ on $\mathbb{R}$. The
quantile coupling $\gamma^\uparrow = (Q_\mu, Q_\nu)_\#\, \mathrm{Leb}_{(0,1)}$
exists for arbitrary $\mu, \nu$ and is the canonical order-preserving
(comonotone) coupling. (Standard; see Santambrogio, *Optimal Transport for
Applied Mathematicians*, Ch. 2.)

**Fact 2 (uniqueness, under the order selection, for atomless sources).** If
$\mu$ is atomless, then $T = Q_\nu \circ F_\mu$ is the unique nondecreasing map
with $T_\# \mu = \nu$, up to $\mu$-null sets. The target may be atomic — this
course's two-point distribution is generated by exactly such a map, and the
full proof is in [The Deterministic Map, Proved](./06-map-proved.qmd)
(Theorem 1 and Propositions 2 and 7 there).

**Fact 3 (optimality, for free).** The same monotone map is optimal for *every*
convex displacement cost $c(x - y)$ — a universality that is essentially
one-dimensional and will *fail* upstairs.

**Fact 4 (the honest direction of the atomic caveat).** The failure mode is not
generation into atomic targets — that always works — but deterministic
*encoding out of* atomic sources: a source atom cannot be split by a map, so no
deterministic encoder carries atomic data onto a continuous prior. The
canonical repair is stochastic — Rüschendorf's *distributional transform*
$U = F_\mu(X^-) + V\,(F_\mu(X) - F_\mu(X^-))$ with $V \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$
independent, which is exactly uniform even when $X$ has atoms. (Randomized
rank-breaking of ties: the coin flip of the informal tutorial.)

So the precise sense in which dimension one is "completely understood":
**order-compatible transport on the line has an explicit, generalized-quantile
solution in all cases.** Not solved by this: transport under other selections,
statistical estimation, or learnability — distinctions that matter below.

## Dimension two and above: underdeterminacy, and the selection principles

Endpoint marginals never determine a coupling: if $T_\# \rho = \mu$ and
$S_\# \rho = \rho$, then $(T \circ S)_\# \rho = \mu$. In $d \ge 2$ the supply
of source-preserving maps $S$ is enormous, and — the genuine loss — no total
order exists to privilege one choice. There is a second, subtler
underdeterminacy at the level of *dynamics*: for the continuity equation
$\partial_t p + \nabla\!\cdot(p v) = 0$, if $v$ transports the path
$\{p_t\}$ then so does $v + w$ for any $w$ with $\nabla\!\cdot(p w) = 0$ —
weighted divergence-free "gauge" fields, abundant in $d \ge 2$, invisible in
$d = 1$ (no room to swirl on a line). Even a prescribed marginal path does not
determine particle trajectories; a *current* must be chosen too.

Each classical and each modern construction is a **selection principle** —
something added to the marginal-matching requirement to pin down a map, a
coupling, or a path. The audit table (each row's qualification is part of the
claim):

| Construction | What selects | Essential qualification |
|---|---|---|
| **Brenier / optimal transport** | minimize squared displacement | unique map $T = \nabla \phi$, $\phi$ convex, for absolutely continuous sources with second moments — canonical *relative to Euclidean quadratic geometry* (Brenier 1991; McCann 1995) |
| **Knothe–Rosenblatt** | sequential conditional quantiles | unique monotone *triangular* map after fixing a coordinate order; not rotation-invariant, generally not optimal (Rosenblatt 1952; Knothe 1957; Carlier–Galichon–Santambrogio 2009) |
| **Autoregressive flows** | triangular architecture + likelihood | an expressive monotone triangular flow can recover KR; permuted stacks need not equal any single KR map (Irons et al. 2022) |
| **General normalizing flows** | architecture, orientation, optimization | maximum likelihood identifies the *density*, not the map |
| **Diffusion / probability-flow ODE** | forward SDE + schedule + score + **choice of current** | the path $\{p_t\}$ alone does not fix the velocity in $d \ge 2$; the gradient-form (curl-free relative to $p$) current is part of the selection |
| **Flow matching / rectified flow** | endpoint coupling + interpolant + regression | different couplings/interpolants give different fields with identical endpoints (Lipman et al. 2023; Liu et al. 2023) |
| **GAN** | *none* | any transport fooling the discriminator is accepted; even WGAN's optimal-transport problem lives between the real and generated laws in data space — it does not select a latent-to-data map (Goodfellow et al. 2014; Arjovsky et al. 2017) |
| **VAE** | ELBO + prior + decoder noise + architecture | selects a generally *nonidentifiable* joint model and posterior kernel, not a Monge map |
| **Schrödinger bridge** | path-space relative entropy to a reference process | the principled *stochastic* transport selection (Léonard 2014) |

And the statistics community, needing multivariate quantiles for its own
reasons, ran the same route: the **center-outward distribution functions** of
Chernozhukov–Galichon–Hallin–Henry (2017) and Hallin et al. (2021,
[arXiv:1806.01238](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.01238)) *define* the multivariate
CDF as the Brenier map to a reference spherical law — canonical relative to
that chosen reference geometry, not choice-free. The lesson of the whole table
in one line: **beyond dimension one, "the transport" is a category mistake;
only "the transport selected by ⟨rule⟩" is well-posed.**

## The 1-D coincidences, stratified by epistemic status

The folklore says "all families coincide with the quantile map in 1-D." The
truth splits three ways, and the split is the pedagogy.

**Theorem-level (all exact scalar ODE samplers — one proof covers them).** Let
$\{p_t\}$ be a smooth positive scalar density path with velocity $v$ solving
the continuity equation with zero flux at $-\infty$. Then
$\partial_t F_t = -p_t v_t$, and along any characteristic
$\dot X = v_t(X)$: $\frac{d}{dt} F_t(X_t) = 0$ — quantile labels are conserved,
so the endpoint map is the quantile transport. This single argument covers the
diffusion probability-flow ODE (proved in full, with numerics, in
[The Deterministic Map, Proved](./06-map-proved.qmd)), continuous normalizing
flows, flow matching, and rectified flow *at the exact/population level*; the
distinctions among them are about how $p_t$ and $v_t$ are chosen and estimated,
not about the exact 1-D endpoint. Monotone discrete-time flows join by
Fact 2 directly. (Practical training adds estimation and integration error —
conditionality of practice, not of mathematics.)

**Available-but-not-selected (GANs).** An explicit counterexample: with
$U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$, the tent map $s(u) = 2u \wedge (2 - 2u)$
preserves uniformity, so $Q_\mu(s(U))$ generates $\mu$ *exactly* — and is not
the quantile map. No idealized adversarial objective can distinguish it from
$Q_\mu(U)$: marginal matching leaves the generator unidentified. The
coincidence is available to a GAN and never implied by its training.

**Available-only-in-a-singular-idealization (VAEs).** The precise proposition:
if data and latent are scalar and atomless, the prior has continuous strictly
increasing CDF $H$, the encoder $E$ and decoder $D$ are *deterministic*, mutually
inverse a.e., aggregate-matched ($E_\# \mu = $ prior), *nondecreasing*, and
exactly optimized, then Fact 2 forces
$E = H^{-1} \circ F_\mu$ and $D = Q_\mu \circ H$ — with a uniform prior,
literally $E = F_\mu$, $D = Q_\mu$. Every hypothesis earns its place: drop
monotonicity and the decreasing solution (and worse) appears; and a *strict*
VAE cannot even enter this idealization — a deterministic encoder against a
continuous prior has infinite KL penalty
($\mathrm{KL}(\mathcal{N}(E(x), \sigma^2) \,\|\, \mathcal{N}(0,1)) \to \infty$
as $\sigma \downarrow 0$), and an expressive decoder admits *posterior
collapse* ($p_\theta(x \mid z) = p_{\text{data}}$, encoder carrying no
information) which fits the marginal perfectly with no CDF anywhere.
Identifiability theory does not rescue the slogan: the identifiable-VAE results
of Khemakhem et al. (2020) require auxiliary observed variables and structured
priors, deliver identification only up to linear/permutation ambiguities, and
do not apply to the ordinary unconditional VAE — consistent with the classical
nonidentifiability of nonlinear ICA (Hyvärinen–Pajunen 1999) and the
impossibility results for unsupervised disentanglement (Locatello et al.
2019). The idealized object is better named a *monotone scalar normalizing
flow* (or a Wasserstein-autoencoder-style construction, whose objective —
Tolstikhin et al. 2018 — does regularize the aggregate encoding, unlike the
VAE's). The slogan "the encoder is the CDF" is a theorem about that idealized
object and a *false statement about VAE training*.

The three-way split generalizes into the distinction this tutorial exists to
teach:

> For any generative method, ask three separate questions. **(1) Existence:**
> can it represent a transport achieving the target law? **(2) Selection:**
> does its construction single out *which* transport? **(3) Identification:**
> does its *training objective* actually enforce that selection? In 1-D, exact
> scalar ODE methods answer yes–yes–yes (order is built into non-crossing);
> GANs answer yes–no–no; VAEs answer yes–no–no with an extra obstruction
> (kernels, not maps). The families feel identical in 1-D only if one asks
> question (1) alone.

## What breaks upstairs: the misleading-intuitions inventory

Each entry is a 1-D truth that fails in $d \ge 2$ — with the failure's
certificate.

1. **"Transport is unique."** Never was — uniqueness belonged to the order
   selection, which does not exist upstairs.
2. **"Non-crossing implies the canonical map."** In $d \ge 2$ trajectories can
   rotate and swirl without intersecting; orientation-preserving
   diffeomorphisms need not be (cyclically) monotone or optimal.
3. **"A gradient velocity field integrates to a gradient map."** False:
   time-ordered products of symmetric Jacobians lose symmetry when Hessians at
   different times fail to commute. This is precisely the mechanism of
   **Lavenant–Santambrogio (2022)** ([Appl. Math. Lett.](https://hal.science/hal-04134092)):
   a smooth two-dimensional example where the Fokker–Planck flow map is a
   perfectly valid transport to the Gaussian and *not* the Brenier map —
   written to refute a published conjecture (Khrulkov–Oseledets 2022) that
   assumed otherwise. The 1-D coincidence misled professionals in print.
4. **"The marginal path determines the particle paths."** Only on the line,
   where zero-flux kills the ambiguity. Upstairs, divergence-free currents are
   a genuine gauge freedom; the diffusion velocity is a *choice* of current.
5. **"Componentwise CDFs are a multivariate rank."** They uniformize marginals
   and leave the entire dependence structure (the copula) untouched;
   Rosenblatt's transform fixes this at the price of coordinate-order
   dependence.
6. **"Monotone becomes meaningless."** It becomes *plural*: coordinatewise
   isotonicity, monotone operators, triangular monotonicity, and cyclic
   monotonicity are inequivalent notions — and different selection principles
   commit to different ones (Brenier: cyclic; KR: triangular).
7. **"One map is optimal for all convex costs."** Essentially one-dimensional.
   Upstairs the selected map depends on the cost and the geometry.
8. **"Low-dimensional pictures scale."** $\|Z\| \approx \sqrt{d}$ for
   $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$ — mass lives on shells, not at the mode; and
   empirical transport estimation suffers dimension-dependent rates of order
   $n^{-1/d}$ (Weed–Bach 2019). The 1-D laboratory is a laboratory, not a
   scale model.

## A short history, as the pedagogy's spine

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1781 | Monge poses the transport problem (déblais et remblais) |
| 1942 | Kantorovich relaxes maps to couplings — transport becomes tractable |
| 1952 / 1957 | Rosenblatt's transformation; Knothe's rearrangement — the coordinate-order selection |
| 1991 / 1995 | Brenier's polar factorization; McCann's refinements — the cost selection, uniqueness restored in $d \ge 2$ |
| 2013–2014 | VAEs (Kingma–Welling); GANs (Goodfellow et al.) — learned transports with variational and adversarial objectives, no map selection |
| 2015–2017 | Normalizing flows mature (Rezende–Mohamed; autoregressive = triangular ≈ KR); WGAN imports the OT *metric* (not the OT map) |
| 2015–2021 | Diffusion: nonequilibrium thermodynamics (Sohl-Dickstein et al.), DDPM (Ho et al.), score SDE and probability-flow ODE (Song et al.) — the dynamic selection |
| 2017–2021 | Statistics rebuilds the CDF via transport: Monge–Kantorovich depth, center-outward distribution functions (Chernozhukov et al.; Hallin et al.) |
| 2022 | Khrulkov–Oseledets conjecture the diffusion flow is OT; **Lavenant–Santambrogio refute it** — the 1-D coincidence formally dies in $d \ge 2$ |
| 2022–2023 | Flow matching (Lipman et al.), rectified flow (Liu et al.), stochastic interpolants (Albergo–Boffi–Vanden-Eijnden) — the coupling-and-interpolant selection made explicit |

The pedagogy of this course tracks that history in miniature: quantiles first,
then the loss of order, then the selections — and the stochastic-interpolant
viewpoint, in which coupling, interpolant, velocity, and noise are all explicit
choices, is where the modern account closes the loop.

## The refined thesis

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## What we actually teach

Many generative samplers can be represented as maps or stochastic kernels
carrying a reference law to the model law — a useful common language, not a
complete characterization of generative modeling. On the real line, the total
order selects a canonical quantile coupling; for atomless sources it is induced
by the unique nondecreasing map, which is simultaneously optimal for every
convex displacement cost. Other transports exist even there. In higher
dimensions, endpoint marginals underdetermine both the coupling and the
dynamics, so additional structure — a cost and its geometry (Brenier), a
coordinate order (Knothe–Rosenblatt, autoregressive flows), a forward
corruption process together with a choice of probability current (diffusion),
an endpoint coupling and interpolant (flow matching, rectified flow,
stochastic interpolants), path-space entropy (Schrödinger bridges), or merely
an architecture and an objective (GANs, VAEs) — selects the construction.
Exact scalar ODE samplers necessarily implement the quantile map, because
non-crossing on a line *is* the order selection; adversarial and variational
objectives do not select it, and stochastic decoders and reverse SDEs are
kernels, not inverse maps. Dimension one is therefore a **laboratory for
separating four questions** — endpoint matching, transport selection, dynamics,
and learnability — not a setting in which the model families are intrinsically
identical.
:::
